Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03837
2 — Intellectual Development
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03838
This social development was clearly reflected in the different forms of culture that could arise in a society living under such historical conditions.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03839
These forms of culture, however, did not all develop to the same degree, and they did not all reflect social reality in the same way.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03840
The first chapter allows us to draw the following broad conclusions.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03841
First: Poetry and language were more highly developed than the other forms of culture found in pre-Islamic society.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03842
This suggests that both had deeper roots in the peninsula’s older history, when parts of Arabia had reached a relatively high level of development.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03843

The clearest evidence comes from the south of the peninsula, especially Yemen, where historically known states such as Sabaʾ, Maʿīn, and Ḥimyar had developed advanced forms of civilization going back to the period before the Common Era.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03844
For reasons that historians have still not been able to explain with confidence, a historical break occurred between that ancient past and the pre-Islamic society of the sixth century CE.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03845
This break cast a long shadow over the economic and social conditions of the sixth century, which appeared in much less developed forms.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03846
Yet poetry and language do not reflect that decline in the same way.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03847
These two parts of pre-Islamic culture had developed far beyond the other areas of life around them.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03848
Second: Pre-Islamic knowledge consisted mainly of scattered and unsystematic results drawn from direct sensory experience and simple forms of reasoning.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03849
Such knowledge developed through everyday contact with nature and with the cosmic phenomena visible to people and directly affecting their lives.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03850
It also developed through the particular social relations in which people lived.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03851
Those relations produced specific customs, traditions, and customary legal practices that served among them much the same purpose that formal laws served in more developed societies.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03852
Third: Of all the forms of consciousness found in pre-Islamic society, religion was the most strongly affected by changes in people’s material life.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03853
As long as the primitive tribal system remained dominant, dividing society into tribal communities based on blood and kinship in their narrowest form, paganism remained the dominant religion.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03854
This was because paganism reflected, in religious consciousness, the structure of the tribal world itself.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03855
The human world was divided into many small and fragmented communities, and pagan religion reflected that same pattern.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03856
It did so in two ways.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03857
First, paganism gave a simple and early form to the relationship between human beings and the natural forces and phenomena that directly affected their daily lives.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03858
It presented those forces as holding absolute, fixed, and unavoidable power over human beings.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03859
Second, paganism rested on a multiplicity of gods that reflected the multiplicity of separate tribal communities.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03860
But shortly before Islam, pre-Islamic society began to undergo changes in its social structure.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03861
Its social relations were starting to move toward a new form of division, one that was preparing the ground for class division.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03862
Religious life began to respond to this wider social transformation.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03863
A movement toward belief in one God now became visible.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03864
It appeared first in Jewish monotheism, which established a base for Judaism in certain regions.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03865
It appeared second in the Christian form of monotheism, which established a base for Christianity in other regions.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03866
Then, toward the end of the pre-Islamic period, a new religious form emerged.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03867
It did not adopt the Jewish or Christian understanding of one God. Instead, it moved toward the understanding of monotheism that would later become Islamic.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03868
This was the religion of the Ḥunafāʾ.
Conclusions of Chapter One
passage-en-03869
At the level of religious consciousness, it was the clearest expression of pre-Islamic Arab society’s growing conflict with its old, fragmented, and plural tribal system.

passage-en-03871
A — The “Class” Reaction
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03872
1 — Muhammad and Quraysh
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03873

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh grew up poor and orphaned, despite belonging to Quraysh. He came from the Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the branch of the Hāshim clan descended from his paternal grandfather. The Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib were among the least wealthy branches of the Hāshim clan, especially the household of Muhammad’s uncle Abū Ṭālib, who took him in during his childhood after the death of his grandfather.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03874

Muhammad began working at an early age, “herding the sheep of the people of Mecca.” He would later say: “Moses was sent as a prophet while he was a shepherd, David was sent while he was a shepherd, and I was sent while I was tending my family’s sheep at Ajyād.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03875
He later worked for Khadīja bint Khuwaylid, who became his first wife, accompanying one of her trading caravans between Mecca and Syria.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03876

The reports that Muhammad had contact with the ḥanīfs seem to have a real basis. He may even have been one of them. There is still a great deal of historical uncertainty surrounding the ḥanīfs as a group, but the historians do give us some clear indications of a close connection between the founder of Islam and this movement. The Qur’an itself also confirms this connection when it describes the ḥanīf faith as the religion of Abraham and presents it as the true religion:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03877
Say: My Lord has guided me to a straight path, a true religion, the faith of Abraham, a ḥanīf, who was not one of the polytheists.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03878
And who is better in religion than one who submits himself to God, does good, and follows the faith of Abraham, a ḥanīf?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03879

This confirms a real connection between Islam and the ḥanīf movement. The movement had emerged in an agricultural region, al-Yamāma, and its preachers had spread into the settled parts of Arabia, especially Mecca. Some of these preachers were prominent figures in pre-Islamic society.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03880

As we argued earlier, the rise of this movement was one expression of the changes taking place in the foundations of social life in pre-Islamic Arabia. The ḥanīf movement was itself one part of a larger set of connected developments. All of them grew out of the broader movement of that society toward change.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03881

And this change could not remain limited to the material foundations of society. It also had to reach the way people understood their world. At that historical stage, this social consciousness took mainly a religious form.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03882

Looking at the rise of Islam in this way, in relation to the conditions of Arab society at the time—and also to the conditions of nearby societies beyond Arabia—helps us see the social and intellectual roots of the major tasks Islam was about to take on.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03883

Islam would play a historically progressive role in carrying out these tasks, changing both the social and intellectual landscape of more than one society, across more than one continent, throughout the Middle Ages.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03884
From the beginning of Muhammad’s mission, it became clear that he stood on a different side from the leaders of Quraysh, at least in the immediate conflict taking shape around him.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03885
Those leaders held material power. They were the great merchants and moneylenders of the Meccan elite, the leading figures associated with the Dār al-Nadwa.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03886

Islam, by contrast, was taking a position that would help drive the movement of change in a progressive direction. In historical terms, this meant helping society move from its earlier and more primitive form of social relations toward a more developed one, in line with what Muruwwa sees as the general objective laws of historical development.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03887
That is why the reaction against Muhammad came so quickly.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03888

At its root, this reaction clearly had a “class” character, even though the conditions for a fully developed class division had not yet matured. The first signs of such a division were, however, becoming increasingly visible, especially in Meccan society. The reaction to the proclamation of Islam was one of the clearest and most revealing of these signs.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03889
Once Muhammad began preaching publicly, the people of Mecca divided broadly into two camps.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03890
On one side were the wealthy: the great merchants, moneylenders, landowners in al-Ṭāʾif, and those who enjoyed privileges connected with control over the pilgrimage and the seasonal markets.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03891
On the other side were the poor: people with no property, hired workers on commercial ventures and caravan journeys, slaves, and oppressed clients of non-Arab origin.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03892
The first group immediately rejected the new message with anger and contempt. At first, they tried temptation and bribery. When that failed, they turned to persecution in its harshest forms.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03893

The second group found in the new message an expression of feelings they had previously been unable to express openly. It gave voice to their vague but real sense of injury caused by social and material inequality, harsh working conditions, and exploitation. The demands imposed by moneylenders and monopolists weighed especially heavily on them.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03894

Some people from this group therefore joined the movement quickly, despite the severe suffering this brought upon them. Others feared the consequences of openly joining it and waited to see how the struggle would end.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03895

From the beginning of his mission, Muhammad condemned those who piled up wealth, consumed the property of orphans and the poor, practiced usury, and monopolized basic necessities. He also condemned the worship of idols and the belief in many gods.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03896
The leaders of Quraysh therefore saw in the new message the specter of a social and intellectual revolt.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03897

If the movement succeeded, it would first destroy the pagan religious status of the Kaʿba, which was also a major center of trade attracting people from across Arabia and beyond. The religious importance of the Kaʿba was closely tied to its commercial importance.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03898
Second, it would threaten the privileges of the Quraysh leadership, privileges that were fundamentally economic and political.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03899
2 — Monotheism and Resurrection
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03900

The Qur’anic verses spoke for the new message. Their literary power reached the highest level of expression familiar to the people of the time, whose appreciation of poetry and eloquence was highly developed by the standards of that period.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03901

It was therefore natural that the Qur’an’s style would appeal strongly to their aesthetic sense. They were struck by the force of its language, the beauty of its composition, and the precision of its references to the stories and laws of earlier peoples, as well as to the traditions, customs, and way of life of pre-Islamic Arabia.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03902
At times they said Muhammad was a poet. At other times they called him a sorcerer. Some went even further in trying to discredit him and called him mad.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03903
In its Meccan verses and surahs, the Qur’an centered its message on two main ideas:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03904
monotheism and resurrection.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03905
As for monotheism, what concerns us here is not its religious meaning as an article of faith. That belongs to another field of study.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03906
What concerns us is what lies beneath that religious meaning: the social dimension of monotheism.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03907

The ḥanīfs had already expressed something of this social meaning, but only in a broad and general way. They could not yet bring its specific form into full view because the ḥanīf movement appeared at a time when the forces breaking apart the tribal order were still only beginning to develop.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03908
By the time Islam appeared, however, the breakdown of the tribal order had become a real historical necessity.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03909

And the need was no longer simply to destroy the old order. The economic, social, political, and intellectual conditions had matured far enough that two tasks now stood side by side: the collapse of the tribal system and the creation of another system to replace it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03910
This new system would need political, legal, and intellectual structures capable of responding to the changes already taking place in the material foundations of society and in social relations.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03911
At the center of those changes was a change in the division of labor.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03912

That change, in turn, required society to be organized on a new basis. People could no longer be divided simply by tribal belonging, as though their place in the production of society’s material needs did not matter.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03913
The division of Arabia into separate and largely independent tribal units had become a real obstacle to the next stage of historical development.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03914
That obstacle therefore had to be broken through.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03915

A unifying framework had to emerge, one capable of containing the new kinds of social conflict that were developing. It had to exist first as a real material force that could unite people, and second as a unifying idea at the level of consciousness.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03916
Islam provided exactly this kind of presence on both levels: as an institution and material force, and as an idea, principle, and belief.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03917
This, in Muruwwa’s view, was the social meaning of monotheism beneath its immediate religious meaning as an Islamic belief.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03918
Many Qur’anic verses point in this direction:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03919

He has laid down for you the same religion that He commanded Noah to follow, and that We have revealed to you, and that We commanded Abraham, Moses, and Jesus to follow: uphold the religion and do not divide over it. (Surat al-Shūrā, verse 14)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03920
Obey God and His Messenger, and do not quarrel with one another, or you will lose heart and your strength will leave you. Be patient; God is with those who are patient. (Surat al-Anfāl, verse 46)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03921
Do not be like those who divided and fell into disagreement after clear proofs had come to them. (Surat Āl ʿImrān, verse 105)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03922

Hold firmly, all together, to the rope of God, and do not divide. Remember God’s favor to you: you were enemies, and He brought your hearts together, so that by His grace you became brothers. (Surat Āl ʿImrān, verse 103)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03923
Muhammad gave this social dimension of monotheism a clear and direct expression in the first political document he issued after the migration to Medina.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03924
The document set out the first principles for cooperation among the different groups living in the city, of whom the Muslims were now one part.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03925

It took the form of a written agreement. Muhammad “wrote an agreement between the Emigrants and the Helpers in which he made peace with the Jews, entered into a covenant with them, confirmed them in their religion and property, and laid down mutual rights and obligations.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03926
The document begins:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03927

“This is a document from Muhammad the Prophet between the believers and Muslims of Quraysh and Yathrib, and those who follow them and fight alongside them: they are one community apart from all other people...”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03928
This is the first principle of the document.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03929
And it points toward the historical direction society was taking: a movement away from the loose, quantitative gathering of separate tribal groups and toward the relations of a larger urban society.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03930
As for the belief in resurrection, which formed the second main axis of the Islamic message, the Qur’an’s own use of the word can help us uncover the social meaning behind it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03931
The Qur’an repeatedly describes the “Day of Resurrection” as the “Day of Dīn.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03932
If we look at the meaning of the word dīn in the Arabic of the period when the Qur’an first appeared, we find that among its meanings were “reckoning,” “judgment,” and “recompense.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03933
The Day of Resurrection, then, is the day when people will be called to account in the world to come for everything they did in this earthly world, the world of human life.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-03934

Behind the metaphysical meaning of the belief in resurrection, there is therefore a social meaning rooted in human life itself and in the real relationships people have with one another in the material world.
